PlantGen · plant_gen

PlantGen documentation

PlantGen grows perennial plants in Blender: stems, leaves, flowers and fruit from a growth simulation, shaped by physics, with a leaf generator and a flower generator for their meshes. Start with the tutorials, look up a task in the how-to guides, read the explanations for why it works the way it does, and use the reference for every one of the 363 controls.

Your first plant

Tutorial

This tutorial takes you from an empty scene to a grown, leafy, flowering plant with welded stems. It is one path with no choices. You need one leaf mesh and one flower mesh. The Leaf Generator and Flower Generator tutorials make them if you have none.

1. Open the panel

In the 3D viewport press N to open the sidebar and click the PlantGen tab. The first panel is Plant Generator.

2. Add a plant

  1. Click Add Plant.
  2. Type a name, Poppy, and click OK.

PlantGen grows a plant at the 3D cursor from the Generic perennial preset. It puts everything in a Poppy_Plant collection, with two empty folders inside it, Poppy_Leafassets and Poppy_Flowerassets. The plant's flower component, Replace Me, draws from the second; it shows nothing until a flower is in the folder.

3. Give it leaves

PlantGen places your leaf mesh. It does not invent the blade.

  1. Make or import one leaf, flat in the XY plane with its face up (+Z), its base at the origin and its tip along +Y.
  2. Drag it into the Poppy_Leafassets folder.

The plant redraws with that leaf at every leaf position.

4. Give it flowers

  1. Make or import one flower, facing +Z with its base at the origin.
  2. Drag it into Poppy_Flowerassets.

A flower now sits at the tip of the stem and of every branch, 12 in all. They come from the plant's flower component, Replace Me in the Components tree, which Add Plant made to draw from Poppy_Flowerassets on every level. Rename it to what it holds (double-click it in the tree).

5. Move through the year

Day is the day of the plant's year it is grown to. A new plant starts at Day 270, fully grown. The Generic perennial comes up on Day 90.

  1. Set Day to 120. The plant is a 0.08 m shoot with 10 nodes.
  2. Set it to 200. It stands 0.54 m with 83 nodes.
  3. Set it back to 270, the full-grown 0.61 m plant.

Live Update is on, so the plant regrows a moment after each change.

6. Weld the stems

  1. Open the Physiology panel and its Surface fold.
  2. Click Weld.

The weld runs in the background and you can keep working. When it lands, every stem and branch is one watertight mesh with filleted junctions and UVs.

7. Render

Frame the plant with your camera and render. Stems, leaves and flowers are geometry like any other object.

You have grown a plant from a preset. The how-to guides go further: give it branches, place leaves with components, vary a setting along the plant with a map, rig it for a game engine. The explanations cover how the growth works.

Your first flower

Tutorial

This tutorial builds a flower with the Flower Generator, bakes it into bud to open stages, and puts those stages on the plant from Your first plant. Each flower on the plant then shows the stage its own openness calls for, so buds, half-open and open flowers grow side by side.

1. Add a flower

  1. In the PlantGen tab open Flower Generator and click Add Flower.
  2. Leave the new flower selected. The panel shows Editing: and its name.

The flower sits in a collection of its own. The panel edits whichever flower is selected.

2. Shape the petals

  1. Open Petals.
  2. In Corolla Type pick Rotate / Wheel, a flat open flower. The other presets range from Tubular and Bell to Cruciform; each sets how the petals fuse and spread.
  3. In Placement set Count to 5.
  4. In Outline raise Length until the petals reach past the disc.

3. Close and open it

  1. Open Bloom and drag Bloom from 1 to 0. The flower folds into a bud.
  2. Drag it back to 1.

Maturity, under it, scales the whole flower over its life and is separate from how open it is.

4. Bake the bloom stages

  1. In Bloom set Stages to 5.
  2. Click Bake Bloom Stages.

PlantGen writes five copies of the flower, from fully closed to fully open, into the shared PlantGen_FlowerAssets collection, named in that order.

5. Put the flowers on the plant

  1. Select the plant from Your first plant.
  2. In Components, select its flower component, Replace Me unless you renamed it.
  3. In the component's settings set Collection to PlantGen_FlowerAssets.

The plant redraws its flowers from the five stages. The Generic perennial forms its first flower on Day 150, at the tip of the stem, and by Day 220 all 12 tips carry one. From Day 275 they turn to fruit. Each flower shows the stage that matches how far it has opened.

A flower component's collection is one bloom sequence, so keep one flower's stages in it. Bake a second flower into a collection of its own.

You have made a flower and grown it on a plant. Make a nodding flower head and Make a hanging raceme arrange flowers on the stem, and the reference lists every Flower Generator control.

Your first leaf

Tutorial

This tutorial makes a toothed, drooping leaf with the Leaf Generator and puts it on the plant from Your first plant. The generator builds the blade from an outline curve, so you need no texture.

1. Switch to Generate

  1. In the PlantGen tab open Leaf Generator.
  2. Set Mode to Generate.

Cutout is the other mode. It cuts leaves from a texture atlas, one leaf per opaque region of the image.

2. Set the outline

  1. Pick a Leaf Shape. It loads its outline into the Profile Curve and sets Width from that shape's proportion. The reference draws all 25 under Leaf Generator › Leaf Shape, and every margin under Margin.
  2. Set Length to 0.12 m.

The profile curve is the half outline, base on the left, tip on the right. Drag its points to change the blade's silhouette.

3. Give it teeth and droop

  1. Open Margin and pick Serrate. Set Teeth to 14.
  2. Open Deform and set Gravity to 0.4. The tip sags under the blade's own weight.
  3. Set Cup to 0.2. The two edges lift into a shallow gutter.

4. Make the leaf

Click Generate Leaf. A new leaf object appears, flat along +Y from the origin, which is the layout the plant expects. While it is selected the panel edits it live.

5. Put it on the plant

  1. Drag the new leaf into the plant's Poppy_Leafassets folder.
  2. Remove the old leaf from that folder.

Every leaf position picks one mesh from the folder at random, so with both in it the plant would mix them.

You have made a leaf and grown it on a plant. To mix several leaf meshes and choose between them by age or shade, see Choose between mesh variants with Traits. The leaf's material is in the generator's Material fold and in Texturing.

Shape the branching with levels

How-to

For changing how many stems a plant has, which branches it grows, at what angle and how long. The numbers below are measured on the Generic perennial at Day 270, which has one stem and 11 branches leaving it at 48 degrees.

The branching is a stack of levels in the Components tree. The Stems level is the plant's stems; a Branches level under it is the branches on those stems, and a level under that is the branches on the branches. Select a level in the tree to see its settings below it.

More stems

Select the Stems level and raise Stems. At 3 the plant has three stems, and each carries its own branches: 33 in all. Spread sets how far apart the stems stand at the ground, and Splay how far they lean out from vertical.

A wider or narrower branch angle

Select the Branches level and set Splay, the angle each branch leaves its stem at, measured from vertical. At 75 the branches leave at 75 degrees. Phyllotaxis sets how the branches turn round the stem from node to node.

Shorter branches

On the Branches level lower Growth. At 50% each branch is the lower half of its full length, 0.08 m instead of 0.16 m, and still flowers at its cut tip. Steps sets how many nodes a full branch has.

Branches only on the lower part of the stem

  1. Select the Branches level and find Masks at the bottom of its settings.
  2. Click + and pick Height.
  3. Set Min to 0 and Max to 0.5.

The plant keeps the branches whose bud sits in the lower half of its height and grows 7 instead of 11. A rejected bud never grows, so the plant does not carry or bend under the missing branches.

Branches on the branches

Select the Branches level, click + and pick Branches. A new level appears under it with its own settings.

To vary a level setting from branch to branch, map it: click the map icon beside the setting. Vary a parameter across the plant with a map covers it. The explanation Levels and components covers how the stack and the components fit together.

Place organs with components

How-to

For putting leaves, bracts, flowers, buds and fruit on a plant, choosing which parts of the plant each kind goes on, and mixing several meshes. A component is one collection of meshes of one organ type, placed on one or more levels.

You supply the meshes. A component places them; it does not model them.

Add a component

  1. In Components, select where it goes in the tree: the Plant row for every level, or one level.
  2. Click +, then New Component, and pick the type: Leaf, Bract, Flower, Bud or Fruit.
  3. In its settings set Collection to the collection holding its meshes.

Each point the component takes gets one mesh from the collection, picked at random. Seed reshuffles that pick for this component alone.

Put it on other levels

Select a level and pick the component from +, or select the component and use Move To in the down-arrow menu beside the tree. A component on several levels is one component: its settings are shared. Components on no level are listed under Not Placed and draw nothing.

Choose where its instances go

Placement lists where instances go, and several can be on at once:

  • On organs uses the organ points growth makes, leaves at nodes and flowers on the inflorescence.
  • Nodes, Internodes, Terminal and Intersections place along the stems at those positions.
  • Random scatters a set count over the stems.
  • Basal makes a rosette of Basal Count leaves (8 by default) at the foot of every stem.

Keep it off part of the plant

Masks decide which points a component takes.

  1. In the component's Masks, click + and pick an attribute, for example Height.
  2. Set Min and Max. A point outside the band goes to another component of the same type that takes it. A point no component takes shows nothing.

Classify View plots the component's points on two attributes, X and Y, and lets you drag its mask window around the ones it should take.

Mix two components on the same points

Give both the same type and placement. Where both may take a point, one is picked at random by Density: two at 1 split the points evenly, 2 against 1 splits them 2:1. Prune deletes a share of a component's own instances at random: 0.5 deletes about half, 1 deletes all.

Leaf and bract extras

Leaf and bract components also have Sky (turn each face toward the sky), Emerging (how a young leaf is curled before it opens), a Petiole fold for a stalk, and Collision, which turns leaves out of each other's way.

To choose between meshes inside one collection by age, height or shade instead of at random, see Choose between mesh variants with Traits.

Vary a parameter across the plant with a map

How-to

For making a setting change from branch to branch, leaf to leaf or flower to flower: longer branches low down, smaller leaves near the tip, a random spread of flower sizes.

Almost every numeric setting of the plant, a level or a component has a map icon beside it. A filled icon means the setting is mapped.

Add a map

  1. Click the map icon beside the setting.
  2. Pick a mode from the menu:
    • Along Height multiplies the setting by 1.25 at the base of the plant, 1 halfway up and 0.75 at the top.
    • By Age runs from 0.75 on the first-made parts to 1.15 on the last.
    • Random Range gives each element its own value between 0.8 and 1.2 times the setting.
    • Custom Curve starts flat and does nothing until you shape the curve.

The map opens in Mapping & Classification, under the part it belongs to, with its settings below the list.

As a worked case, an Along Height map on the Branches level's Length › Start makes the Generic perennial's lowest branch 1.22 times as long, 0.177 m instead of 0.145 m, and its highest 0.86 times, 0.185 m instead of 0.214 m.

Change what drives it

In the map's settings, Driver is the value the curve reads, from 0 to 1: Height, Age, Shade, Node Index, Branch Depth, a custom attribute, a class, or Random. The curve turns that value into a multiplier. Amount blends the map in: 0 is no effect, 1 is the curve in full.

Mode switches the map to another of the four modes.

A setting the plant reads once

Some settings are one value for the whole plant, so there is nothing to vary along. Their map offers Random Range and Per Plant (random), a curve over one random value per plant. The map's settings say how it is evaluated: per plant, per branch, per node, per instance, per leaf or per flower.

Switch a map off or remove it

The checkbox on the map's row in Mapping & Classification switches it off and keeps it. The - button beside the list removes it.

To build your own driver, a distance to an object, a noise or two channels combined, add a Custom Attribute in Mapping & Classification. To reuse a set of masks as one driver, add a Class. The explanation Masks, maps and classes covers how a map changes a value the simulation computes.

Choose between mesh variants with Traits

How-to

For a leaf, bract, bud or fruit component with several meshes in its collection, when the choice should follow the plant: young leaves take the small pale mesh, shaded leaves the dark one, the tip the narrow one. Without Traits each point picks a mesh at random.

Flower components have no Traits. Their meshes are bloom stages, not variants.

Start a sheet

  1. Select the component in Components and open its Traits fold.
  2. Click Add Property. The sheet appears: a row per mesh in the collection, a column for the property.
  3. Pick the column's property in the dropdown above the sheet: Age, Height, Shade, or any other attribute, custom attribute or class.

Weights Only starts a sheet with no columns, to set how common each mesh is and nothing else.

Fill it in

Each row has a Weight and one cell per column.

  • Weight is how common the mesh is. A mesh at 2 is picked twice as often as one at 1; at 0 it is never picked, unless no mesh suits a point.
  • A cell runs from -1 to 1 and scales the mesh's weight at each point by the property's value there, from 0 to 1. At +1 the weight is multiplied by twice the value: 0 where the property is 0, 2 where it is 1. At -1 it is multiplied by twice the remainder, 2 where the property is 0. At 0 the property makes no difference. Values between blend.

A worked case: two leaf meshes, the young one at -1 on Age and the old one at +1. At a point of Age 0.25 the old mesh is picked with chance 0.25 and the young one with 0.75. With several columns, a mesh's chances multiply.

The pick stays random, so neighbouring points still mix. A sheet with every weight equal and every cell 0 picks exactly as no sheet does.

Keep it in step with the collection

When you add or remove meshes in the collection, the sheet shows The collection changed. Click Update Rows: new meshes join with weight 1, and the rows of removed ones go. The bin button clears the sheet.

The sheet belongs to the component, so the same mesh can lean differently in another component or plant. Presets save it.

Make a nodding flower head

How-to

For a single flower or a dense head that bows over on its stem, like a poppy bud or a young sunflower. The numbers below are measured on a new plant (the Generic perennial) at Day 270, with one flower component on the Stems level, so the only flower is at the stem's tip. Each is the angle of the stem's tip from vertical.

A head at the tip of a stem nods because it is heavy and the stem gives. Two settings decide it together: the flower component's Weight and the stems level's Stiffness.

Put one head on the stem

A new plant's flower component, Replace Me, sits on the Plant row and flowers every tip. For one head on each stem:

  1. In Components, select the flower component.
  2. In the down-arrow menu beside the tree, pick Move To and the Stems level.
  3. Set its Collection to the head's mesh.

On the Stems level it flowers the stem's tip only. On the Plant row the branch tips flower too, and those flowers load the stem as well.

Make the head heavy

  1. Select the flower component.
  2. Raise Weight. Its default, 0.0004, barely loads the stem.

Doubling Weight about doubles the nod. Flower mass also grows with the cube of the component's Size: at Stiffness 0.3 and Weight 0.05, Size 1 nods 6°, Size 1.5 nods 18° and Size 2 nods 42°.

Let the stem give

  1. Select the Stems level.
  2. Lower Stiffness. Each 0.1 lower about doubles the nod.

The tip's angle from vertical, by Stiffness and Weight:

StiffnessWeight 0.01Weight 0.05Weight 0.1Weight 0.2
0.51°1°3°5°
0.33°6°11°21°
0.25°12°22°42°
0.111°23°44°85°

At Stiffness 0.1 and Weight 0.2 the head is level. A softer stem or a heavier head hangs it past level.

A thick stem resists bending far more than a thin one, so a stiff base with a nodding tip comes from the stem's taper, set on the Stems level under Width.

If it will not bend

Check the plant is not tiny. The bend comes from mass against stiffness, and on a small, light plant there is little mass to bend with. For flowers along an inflorescence that should point down whatever they weigh, use the pedicel's Angle instead, as Make a hanging raceme shows.

Model the flower or head mesh yourself, or build it with the Flower Generator; PlantGen decides where the head sits and how far it nods, not its shape.

Make a hanging raceme

How-to

For a spike of flowers ranged down one side and pointing down, like a foxglove, or for racemes that hang from the stem as a whole, like laburnum. The numbers below are measured on the Generic perennial at Day 270.

Turn the inflorescence into a raceme

  1. Select the flower component in Components.
  2. Under Inflorescence, set Type to Raceme.

Count sets the flowers per raceme and Spacing how close they sit, as a fraction of the stem's own internode length.

Crowd the flowers onto one side

Lower Spread, the share of the stem's circumference the flowers occupy. At 360 the seven flowers of the main raceme spread over 275 degrees; at 180 over 154 degrees; at 100 they gather onto 85 degrees, one side of the spire.

Point the flowers down

Set the pedicel's Angle negative. 0 holds each pedicel straight out, positive angles it up toward the tip, and negative hangs it: at -70 every pedicel hangs at -70 degrees. The angle works whatever the flower weighs.

Bend curves each pedicel without moving its flower.

Hang the whole raceme from the stem

For racemes that leave the stem at the nodes and hang, laburnum style:

  1. Set Attachment Location to Axillary.
  2. Set Orientation to Pendulous and raise Strength.

With no pull the racemes leave the stem at 86 degrees from vertical. At Strength 0.5 they hang to 128 degrees, at 1 to 150 degrees. The stem's own weight bends them a little further, so even at 1 they are not forced to exactly vertical.

Reach It As Flowers Open makes a raceme arrive at the pendulous direction as it fills with flowers, upright while it is in bud and bowed over once laden.

Open the flowers from the bottom

Order under Bloom sets which flowers open first. Bottom first opens the raceme from its base to its tip, as a foxglove does.

Model the bell or flower mesh yourself, or build it with the Flower Generator.

Grow around obstacles and steer with effectors

How-to

For a plant that leans out from under a table, grows around a rock, or bends toward a point you choose. All of it is in Physiology.

Grow around an obstacle

  1. Put the obstacle meshes in their own collection, for example Obstacles. Closed shapes work best.
  2. Open Physiology › Obstacles and set Collection to it.
  3. Raise Clearance, the distance in metres the growing tips keep from a surface, up to 0.5 m.

Tips curve away as they approach a surface, and a tip that runs out of room stops instead of growing through. At Clearance 0 the plant ignores obstacles. The obstacles also shade the plant.

Lean out of the shade

In Physiology › Light raise Light Seeking. It turns the growing tips toward the light each step, after gravity has had its say, so a shaded shoot leans out from under whatever covers it. At 0 the plant ignores where the light comes from.

Steer by hand with an effector

  1. In Physiology › Effectors click Add Effector. An empty appears at the 3D cursor, linked to the plant.
  2. Select the empty. The Plant Effector panel shows its settings.
  3. Pick a Kind:
    • Attract pulls nearby growth toward it.
    • Repel pushes nearby growth away.
    • Forbid keeps growth out of its sphere; tips that reach the edge stop.
    • Target aims the whole plant at it from any distance; Radius is ignored.
    • Flatten grows the plant in the plane the empty faces, for an espalier or a fan. Rotate the empty to turn the plane.
    • Orbit spirals growth around the empty's axis, for a stem twining up a pole. Pair it with an Attract on the same spot to keep the stem on the pole.
    • Align Up turns each node's leaves and flowers to face the empty. It turns where branches leave too, so a bushy plant shifts as a whole.
    • Level Up turns each node to lie flat in the empty's plane. Rotate the empty to turn the plane.
  4. Set Radius, how far its influence reaches, and Strength, how far a tip turns each step. At Strength 1 a tip aims straight at it every step.

An effector in the plant's effector collection acts at once; there is nothing to switch on first.

After moving things

The plant regrows when you change a setting. When you move the plant, an obstacle or an effector, click Regrow in Plant Generator so the plant grows against where things stand now.

The explanation The environment nudges, it doesn't decide covers why the surroundings only ever adjust growth.

Prune limbs by hand

How-to

For cutting a branch off the grown plant, the way a gardener would, without changing anything else about how it grows.

  1. Open Physiology › Pruning and click Prune Limbs. The button becomes Stop Pruning, and the plant shows a labelled glyph at every node, bud, apex, leaf and flower.
  2. Point at a glyph on the limb you want gone and press X. That limb goes, with every branch, leaf and flower growing from it.
  3. Prune more limbs the same way, then click Stop Pruning.

The fold counts the pruned limbs. Keep Dead Wood leaves a pruned limb standing as grey dead wood instead of removing it. It is off by default, because a cut removes the limb. Clear Pruning brings every pruned limb back.

A prune belongs to the plant's current branching. When a change makes the plant branch differently, the pruned limbs no longer match, so PlantGen drops them, the fold shows Pruning cleared: topology changed, and the plant grows whole again. Prune last, once the branching is settled.

Weld and texture the plant

How-to

For turning the stems into one clean mesh with UVs, giving each level its own bark, and setting up the leaf and flower materials.

Weld the stems

  1. Open Physiology › Surface. Weld Junctions is on by default.
  2. Click Weld.

The weld runs in the background while you keep working, and the button reads Welding... until it lands. Then every stem and branch is one watertight mesh, each junction filleted, with UVs. A junction that cannot be built, such as a branch too short to clear its fillet, stays a capped tube inside its parent. The fold counts the built and the capped junctions. Weld Range sets how round the fillet is, in branch radii, 0.5 by default; 0 leaves a hard crease. Smoothness sets how densely rings sit along the stems; at the default 4 the faces are close to square.

Light Stalks is for a plant with thousands of flowers. It builds pedicels with four sides and gives stems too thin to show bark fewer rings on their straight runs, while branch welds and bends keep their density. Laburnum's stems came to 663,705 vertices with it on, its pedicels 8 vertices each.

A change that regrows the plant drops back to the unwelded preview. Weld again when the plant is settled. A plant you welded before at the same settings shows its weld again without rebuilding it.

Give each level its own stem material

  1. Open Texturing › Materials. The list holds a row per branching level, then every material the leaves and flowers wear.
  2. Select a level's row and pick a material, or click New for a PlantGen stem material (the Green Stem preset, untextured).
  3. Pick a Preset for its look, and open Textures & Settings for its image slots and shader values.

A level without a material of its own wears its parent level's, shown greyed in the list.

Edit the leaf and flower materials

Select a leaf or flower material in the same list. Its preset and Textures & Settings appear below. A material is often shared by several meshes, and an edit changes every mesh that wears it.

Set the texture scale

Texturing › UV › Size is the world size of one texture tile, 0.025 m by default, the same on every stem, branch and stalk, so a thin stalk shows the same size squares as the thickest stem. The checker button beside it shows the stems with a checker texture instead of their material.

The cells stay square along the stem and the branches, and the checker runs on across each joint without a seam in the middle of the fillet.

How the stems unwrap

Each stem and each branch is one UV island, unwrapped round its circumference and along its length, tiling the texture. The weld cuts a hole in the stem's island where the branch leaves; it doesn't move the stem's UVs. The branch's island starts at the joint: its fillet rings flare out to meet the hole's edge, then the plain branch runs on.

Because the islands tile one texture, they overlap in UV space; in Blender's UV editor every stem and branch lies across the same tiles. Use a tiling bark texture, not a baked atlas, on stem materials.

Read the vertex colours

Texturing › Vertex Colors shows the four channels every exported mesh carries, for a game engine's foliage shader:

  • Red rises from 0 at each leaf's base to 1 at its tip, flat on stems and flowers.
  • Green is one random value per leaf or flower.
  • Blue is one random value for the whole plant.
  • Alpha is height up the plant, 0 at the root to 1 at the top.

Click a channel's button to show the plant coloured by it in the viewport; click it again to go back. Vertex Colors shows all four at once. The view is viewport-only; the colours themselves are always on the mesh and export with it.

Rig the plant and export it to Unreal with wind

How-to

For taking a plant into Unreal Engine as a skeletal mesh that sways in the wind. Unreal's Dynamic Wind simulates the sway itself from bone groups that PlantGen writes. No motion is baked or exported. For large plantings, build the rig here and then follow Export a Nanite Assembly to Unreal.

Build the rig

  1. Open Physiology › Rig.
  2. Set Bone Angle for each level: how far a stem may bend along one bone before the next bone starts, 15° by default. Straight runs share a bone and bends get more. At 0 every node gets a bone.
  3. Click Build Rig.

Build Rig welds the stems first, since the rig skins the welded mesh. It then builds a bone chain down every stem and branch and a bone for every leaf, bract, flower, bud and fruit, skins the mesh with smooth weights, and turns on Rig View. The plant you see is now the rigged mesh, and the fold counts the stem and organ bones.

Show Bones draws the skeleton over the plant, and Display sets how it draws. Fast Preview, on by default, moves the leaves and flowers rigidly with their bones so playback stays quick; the export always uses the full mesh.

An edit that regrows the plant drops back to the live plant. The fold then warns in red that the plant changed since the rig was built, and Rig View and Export still show the old plant. Click Build Rig again after the edit.

Preview the wind

  1. Open Physiology › Wind and turn on Bone Wind.
  2. Play the timeline.

Each stem bone bends by its own flexibility, so long thin parts sway most. Strength, Stiffness and the Gusts settings shape this preview only; they never reach Unreal. Vertex Wind adds the leaf-tip flutter that an engine's foliage material makes from the vertex colours, also preview only.

Export

  1. Click Export Rig and give a file name ending in .fbx or .usdc.
  2. PlantGen writes the skeletal mesh in its bind pose with weights, UVs, materials and vertex colours, the plant's root at the origin. Beside it goes <name>_wind.json.

In Unreal

  1. Import the FBX or USD as a skeletal mesh.
  2. Right-click the mesh, choose Scripted Asset Actions > Import Dynamic Wind Data and pick <name>_wind.json.
  3. Create a Dynamic Wind Data asset and tick Enabled.
  4. Place the mesh through an Instanced Skinned Mesh component with that asset as its Transform Provider.
  5. Drag Epic's BP_GlobalFoliageActor_UE5 into the level to drive the wind. Its location is in Export a Nanite Assembly to Unreal.

The wind file puts every bone in a simulation group: the trunk, one group per branching level, the inflorescences, and the organs. The stems of a perennial all go on the trunk. Each other group's influence comes from how flexible its bones are. The Unreal wind groups list at the bottom of the Wind fold shows the groups, their bone counts and their influence. Dynamic Wind is experimental in Unreal 5.7 and blows from one global direction.

Export a Nanite Assembly to Unreal

How-to

For taking a plant into Unreal Engine 5.7 as a Nanite Assembly with wind, the export to use for large plantings. The stems become one skinned mesh. Each leaf and flower becomes an instance of its component's mesh, tied to its own bone. Rudbeckia fulgida exports as a 37,266-vertex base mesh and 267 instances of 13 meshes on 364 bones. These steps were tested in Unreal 5.7.4.

You need a built rig first: Rig the plant and export it to Unreal with wind covers Bone Angle and the Blender wind previews.

Choose the export

Each button in Physiology › Rig writes one model and one wind file.

ButtonWritesUse it for
Export Nanite Assembly<name>_assembly.usdc, <name>_assembly_wind.json, textures/Many plants in Unreal 5.7 or later
Export Rig<name>.fbx or a USD file, <name>_wind.jsonOne ordinary skeletal mesh, with every leaf as unique geometry

Plant Generator › Variations has a third button, also named Export Nanite Assembly. It writes <name>_variations.usdc for a plant and all its built variations, one wind file per plant and textures/. Use it whenever you want more than one variation in Unreal. Unreal shares assets only within one import: ten Rudbeckia fulgida variations made 124 part meshes, 42 materials and 10 textures as ten files, and 13, 4 and 1 as one file. A variation with no current rig gets one for the export and loses it after, so your scene stays as it was. The ten took 5.5 minutes.

The USD file finds its images through a relative path, so keep textures/ beside it. The wind file says how much each bone sways. Exports of the same rig write identical wind files, so one copy is enough. Each plant in a variations file needs its own wind file, because each has its own skeleton.

Set up the Unreal project

Do this once per project.

  1. In Edit > Plugins, enable USD Importer and Procedural Vegetation Editor. The second brings in Dynamic Wind and holds the wind actor.
  2. Leave Interchange OpenUSD off.
  3. In Project Settings > Engine > Rendering > Nanite, turn on Nanite Foliage (Experimental) and restart the editor when asked. The first restart compiles shaders.

Export from Blender

  1. Select the plant and set its Day.
  2. Open Physiology › Rig and click Build Rig.
  3. Click Export Nanite Assembly and save with the extension .usdc.

The export changes four things:

  • A flower takes its nearest bloom stage, up to 2.9 mm away on Rudbeckia fulgida.
  • An organ that matches none of its component's meshes, such as a leaf still unfolding, stays in the base mesh on its own bone.
  • Materials carry the colour texture, colour and roughness. Opacity is left out, because Unreal's USD import makes an opacity material translucent and a translucent material on a Nanite mesh crashes the editor. Leaves and petals must be cut-out meshes, not cards with alpha.
  • The instanced leaves and flowers lose their per-organ vertex colours.

Import into Unreal

  1. In the Content Drawer, click Import and pick the .usdc.
  2. Keep Geometry and Materials & Textures on. Turn off Actors, Skeletal Animations and LevelSequences.
  3. Click Save All. The new assets exist only in memory until you save.

The import creates SK_root, the assembly, and one SK_PGS_Proto_* mesh per part, in a SkeletalMeshes folder. A variations file names each assembly after its plant instead, such as SK_Rudbeckia_fulgida_var_001, and the parts are shared between them. The SK_*_Rig meshes are a step of Unreal's import that nothing uses afterwards. On the ten variations they are 102 of 154 MB.

Keep the flowers at a distance

Nanite removes thin parts as it simplifies a distant mesh, so set this on every mesh or the flowers fade out. USD cannot store the setting.

  1. Open each SK_PGS_Proto_* mesh and set Nanite Settings > Shape Preservation to Voxelize. A part builds from its own settings.
  2. Do the same on SK_root last, then save. In a variations import, do every assembly last.

On a field of 10,000 Rudbeckia fulgida plants, yellow fell from 40% of the plant's pixels at 10 m to 0.8% at 200 m without Voxelize. With Voxelize it held 46-56% at every distance, and frame time stayed within about 1 ms on an RTX 2080.

Add the wind

  1. Right-click SK_root and choose Scripted Asset Actions > Import Dynamic Wind Data. Pick <name>_assembly_wind.json, then save. In a variations import, do this once per assembly, each with its own plant's file.
  2. Create a Dynamic Wind Data asset in the Content Browser, open it and tick Enabled.

Place the plant

  1. Place an empty Actor and add an Instanced Skinned Mesh component.
  2. Set the component's mesh to SK_root and its Transform Provider to the Dynamic Wind Data asset.
  3. Add one entry to Instances per plant. For a field, fill the list from a Blueprint or Python with Add Instances.
  4. Give the plants different Z rotations. Dynamic Wind simulates 8 poses per skeleton, one per slice of rotation, so plants that share a rotation sway alike. The same limit keeps wind cost flat: it added 0.06 ms at most, with 100,000 plants 40 cm apart running at 64 FPS on an RTX 2080.

Start the wind in the level

Dynamic Wind has no gusts of its own, and without a driver the sway stops and starts.

  1. In the Content Browser settings, turn on Show Plugin Content.
  2. Open ProceduralVegetationEditor/SampleAssets/Materials/GlobalFoliageActor.
  3. Drag BP_GlobalFoliageActor_UE5 into the level. It runs in the editor as well as in play.
  4. Set Wind Speed on the placed actor.

Replace a plant with a new export

Voxelize and the wind data live on the imported meshes. Delete the old import, import the new file, set Voxelize and import the wind data again, and set the mesh on the component again.

Render a growth timelapse

How-to

For an animation of the plant growing from seedling to flowering, where every frame is the real plant on that day.

  1. In Plant Generator open Growth Timelapse and turn on Grow Over Timeline. Day now follows the timeline and shows greyed.
  2. Set Start Day and End Day. The scene's first frame shows Start Day and its last frame shows End Day; the defaults run Day 90 to 300. The fold prints the mapping, for example Frames 1-250 play Day 90 -> 300.
  3. Click Bake Timelapse. PlantGen grows every frame once and records it, so the timeline plays back smoothly. Press Esc to stop; the frames done so far are kept, and the next bake skips them. The fold counts the recorded frames.
  4. Render the animation as usual. A render always regrows each frame exactly.

Each frame is a full regrow, which is why the bake exists. Without it, the first pass over the timeline regrows the plant on every frame. Any edit to the plant clears the recorded frames; the bin button beside Bake clears them by hand.

The scene's frame range sets the pace: 250 frames over Day 90 to 300 is 0.84 days a frame. An End Day past the first season runs into winter, and Lifespan decides what happens there. A Single season plant stays mature, an Annual dies standing at season end, and a Herbaceous perennial dies back each winter and regrows a slightly bigger top each spring.

Make a grid of variations and bake it

How-to

For a row or grid of plants of the same species, each one a different individual, to pick a favourite from or to scatter in a scene.

  1. Select the plant and open Plant Generator › Variations.
  2. Pick a Layout. Row is one row of Plants (10 by default). Grid adds Rows (3 by default).
  3. Set Seed Step, the gap between the plants' seeds. On Seed 0 with Step 100 the plants grow from seeds 100, 200, 300 and so on. Change it for a fresh set.
  4. Pick the setting stepped along the row with the button beside Along the Row. It starts at the plant's own value; set Step, the amount added at each next plant. A new plant steps Day back by 18 from its own Day, so the row runs from the full-grown plant at Day 270 back to a young shoot at Day 108. In a Grid, Across Rows steps a second setting from row to row; leave it empty and the rows differ only by seed.
  5. Click Build 10 Plants. The copies appear in a row to the right of the plant, in a collection of their own.

Auto Spacing spaces the copies by the widest one's footprint plus a quarter. Turn it off to set Spacing X and Spacing Y yourself. Labels writes each copy's stepped values and seed under it. Weld welds every copy as it is built, which is slow; off, the copies show the quick unwelded preview.

The copies are rebuilt from the source plant each time, never edited. Edit the source and click Rebuild. Selecting a copy shows the source's settings. Clear removes the copies.

Bake

Click Bake to Meshes. Every copy becomes one plain mesh object in its own collection: welded, with its leaves, flowers and fruit made real geometry, and no modifiers. Bake welds even when Weld is off. The live copies are hidden, not deleted, so Rebuild and Clear still work on them.

Export to Unreal

Click Export Nanite Assembly in the same fold to write the plant and all its copies as one USD file, so they share their leaf and flower meshes in Unreal. Export a Nanite Assembly to Unreal has the steps.

Save and share a preset

How-to

For keeping a plant you like, reusing it in other files, and sending it to someone else.

A preset is the whole plant. It holds every setting, every level, component, mask, map and curve, and its assets: the component collections with their leaf and flower meshes, the level materials, and their textures. Loading it gives a 1-to-1 copy of the plant you saved.

Save

  1. Select the plant. In Plant Generator, click the save button beside the preset menu.
  2. Give it a Name (shown in the menu) and, if you like, a one-line Description.
  3. Keep the suggested folder and click Save Preset.

PlantGen writes two files of the same name: <name>.json with the settings, and <name>.blend with the assets, textures packed. The suggested folder is your user presets folder, so the preset appears under My presets in the menu. To keep presets somewhere else, such as a shared drive, set User Presets Folder in the add-on's preferences.

Load

  1. Select a plant. Loading a preset replaces all of its settings, so use a new plant (Add Plant) for a preset you only want to look at.
  2. Open the preset menu in Plant Generator and pick a preset under Bundled species or My presets. For a file anywhere else, pick Load from File....

The plant regrows as the preset. The assets come in from the .blend beside the .json; a collection or material the file already has, by name, is used as it is. The menu now shows the preset's name, and the reload button beside it re-applies the preset file, picking up changes made to it since.

Share

Send both files, <name>.json and <name>.blend. The recipient picks Load from File... and opens the .json; the .blend must sit beside it.

To check a preset's growth settings without Blender, run this from the PlantGen folder:

python tools/validate_preset.py <name>.json

It checks that the settings load and save unchanged, prints the plant's size at three ages, and runs the 14 structural checks on the grown plant. It does not look at the .blend.

How a plant grows

Explanation

PlantGen doesn't draw a plant shape and decorate it. It grows the plant, one node at a time, the way a shoot builds itself, and then lets the grown plant bend under its own weight. Knowing the two halves explains most of what the controls do and why some of them only show at certain Days.

The phytomer

A stem is a stack of repeated units botanists call phytomers: a node, the internode below it, the leaf at the node, and a bud in that leaf's axil. Every node PlantGen grows is one of these. There is no way to grow a bare node, so leaves and buds come with the structure rather than being scattered over it afterwards.

Each growth step does the same few things in order. Every growing tip adds a node. Buds that are due break into branches, laid out by the next level's phyllotaxis. Axes that have reached their length end, and an ending tip flowers when a flower component is placed there with Terminal attachment; otherwise it stops or hands on to a relay or a fork, as its level's Growth Pattern says. A branch is an axis like the stem, with its own tip and buds, so the same step builds every level.

The stems level's Steps sets the step count. The Generic perennial grows in 26 steps.

The second half: physical form

Once growth is done, a fixed pass shapes the grown plant without adding or removing anything. It thickens every stem from what it carries, bends the stems and branches under their own weight and the weight of their leaves, flowers and fruit, droops the flower stalks, turns flowers and leaves toward the sun, and marks what is dying back in autumn. The stiffness and weight controls act here (Bend and droop under load). Because this pass never changes what grows where, a bend can't make a branch appear or vanish.

The calendar

Day is a real day of the year, and the plant's development runs on it. The plant comes up on Emergence Day and is full grown Season Length days later. Between the two, development is spread evenly over the days, so the Generic perennial (Emergence Day 90, Season Length 180) grows a step about every 6.9 days:

DayProgressNodesHeight
90000
1200.17100.08 m
1500.33360.26 m
2000.61830.54 m
2701890.61 m

Between two steps the newest node lengthens smoothly, so scrubbing Day shows a growing tip rather than nodes popping in.

Every step reads the calendar at its own Day, never at the Day the plant is grown to. So a plant grown to Day 200 is the Day 150 plant grown further. At Day 150 the Generic plant has 9 axes, and every one of them is still there at Day 200 with at least as many nodes. A timelapse depends on this.

The calendar's windows are counted in days after emergence. The Phenology Calendar edits them as bands:

  • Bloom opens 55 days after emergence and lasts 75 by default. Flowering starts on the bloom date, or later if the plant is not yet big enough to flower. The Generic perennial's bloom window opens on Day 145; its first flower forms on Day 150 and its last tip flowers by Day 220.
  • Fruit opens at 185 days and lasts 95, then the fruit drops.
  • Autumn opens at 180 days and lasts 60: leaves colour and the plant dies back.

Days past the first season are where Lifespan matters. A Single season plant stays mature. An Annual dies standing at season end. A Herbaceous perennial dies back to the ground in winter and comes up again next spring a little bigger. The Generic perennial is one: on Day 400 it shows nothing, and on Day 635, a year after its first full growth, it stands 0.64 m, 5% taller than in its first year.

Why timing controls shift display, not growth

Every organ's random variation (a leaf's size, its yaw, a flower's pitch) is dealt from the order parts are made in. A control that changed when parts are made would re-deal that variation over the whole plant. So Emergence Delay, which makes branches come up later, grows the plant exactly as before and holds the late parts back from view until their day. The full-grown plant is the same either way, and each earlier Day is a part of it.

Levels and components

Explanation

The Components tree holds two kinds of thing. Levels are the plant's woody structure: the stems, the branches on them, the branches on those. Components are what that structure carries: leaves, bracts, flowers, buds and fruit. Each is a separate stack because they answer separate questions. A level says what grows. A component says what it looks like and where it goes.

Levels

Level 0 is the stems. Each level below it is the branches growing on the level above. The Generic perennial has two: one stem, and 11 branches on it.

A level holds everything about its axes: how many and how they turn round their parent (Phyllotaxis), the angles they leave at, how many nodes a full one has (Steps) and how much of that it builds (Growth), how long and thick it is, how stiff, its material, and its own Masks and Maps.

Every node of an axis bears branches of the next level, except the tip node. What continues the tip is the axis itself, a relay or a fork, as the level's Growth Pattern says:

  • Monopodial: one tip builds the whole axis, and branches leave its sides.
  • Sympodial, Dichasial, Pleiochasial: the axis grows in units. Each unit ends, and one, two or a ring of buds below it carry on.
  • Pseudomonopodial (Aligned Relay): a sympodium whose relay continues in line, so it reads as one straight stem.
  • Dichotomous and Pseudomonopodial (Unequal Fork): the tip splits, into equal forks or into a leader and weaker forks.

The deepest level has no level below it. Its leaf-axil buds can only become flowers.

A level has no setting for whether it ends in a flower. That is the flower component's job.

Components

A component is one organ type and one collection of meshes, placed on any set of levels. Placed on the Plant row, it goes on every level.

Where flowers grow is the flower component's Attachment Location. Terminal flowers the tips, including each unit's tip in a sympodium. Axillary, Internodal and Leaf-opposed flower the nodes. Growth only flowers on levels a flower component is placed on. A new plant comes with one, Replace Me, on the Plant row with Terminal attachment, so every tip flowers.

The first component of a type owns growth

Growth needs a single answer to questions like "how far apart are the flowers" and "how heavy is a leaf". It takes them from the first component of each type placed On organs, in list order:

  • The first flower component grows the main inflorescence. A later flower component with Own Inflorescence on grows another one on its own levels; where two want the same tip, the one higher in the list wins. Other flower components draw on the flowers already there.
  • The first leaf component's Phyllotaxis sets how the grown leaves are arranged, and its Weight loads the stems.
  • The first bract component's Size and the first fruit component's Size, Set and Weight are the inflorescence's bracts and fruit.

So reordering components can change the plant, not only its look. Muting a component never does. Mute hides what the component draws and leaves growth alone, including when the muted one is the owner.

Every placed leaf weighs

A leaf is never decoration only. Leaves placed by a component (on Nodes, Random, Basal and so on) add their weight to the stem nodes they sit on, the same as grown leaves. A component's Masks are not counted when working out that weight, and its Prune is counted as an average share.

Seeds

Every level and every component has its own Seed, mixed with the plant's Master Seed. At 0 a level or component follows the master alone. Change one to reshuffle that part only: a new branch layout on one level, or a new mesh pick for one component, with everything else unchanged. Seeds and the same plant twice covers why this works.

Masks, maps and classes

Explanation

PlantGen computes a plant from botany and physics: how fast a shoot grows, how much a stem bends under its load. Masks and maps let you steer that result part by part without replacing it. The split is simple. The simulation computes a value; a map multiplies it; a mask decides whether a part is there at all.

Channels: what every part knows about itself

Every branch, node, leaf and flower carries a set of values from 0 to 1 called channels: how high up the plant it sits (Height), how early it was made (Age), how shaded it is (Shade), its index along its stem, its branch depth, and a random value of its own. Masks and maps read these. A channel is a measurement, not a setting: Height is 0.5 halfway up whatever the plant ends up being.

You can add channels. A custom attribute is a new one: closeness to an object, a 3D noise, or two channels combined. A class is a named set of masks, read as a channel that is 1 on the parts the masks keep and 0 elsewhere. Use a class when several components or maps should agree on the same group of parts, such as "the sunny upper side", defined once.

Masks decide which

A mask keeps the parts whose channel falls in a band, Min to Max, and can invert to keep the outside instead. Several masks combine into one keep value.

Where a mask sits decides what it does to the plant:

  • A level's masks run during growth and decide which branches grow. A rejected bud never grows, so the plant does not carry or bend under it. Keeping Height 0 to 0.5 on the Generic perennial's branches leaves 7 of 11.
  • A component's masks run after growth and decide which points the component draws. The plant is already grown and bent by then, so a masked leaf still counted toward the stem's load; it isn't drawn by this component. Another component of the same type may take the point.

Maps decide how much

A map turns a channel into a multiplier through a curve, and multiplies a setting by it:

value = setting × (1 + Amount × (curve(channel) − 1))

At Amount 0, or with the curve flat at 1, the map does nothing. That is how every map starts.

A map never creates, places or removes anything. It scales a number the simulation was already using. A map on a branch level's Length › Start makes each branch longer or shorter, and growth then carries on as usual with that branch: it bears as many nodes, and its weight bends the stem below it accordingly. An Along Height map there makes the Generic perennial's lowest branch 1.22 times as long and its highest 0.86 times.

When a map is read

A map is read where its setting is used, and that decides what it can see:

  • Growth maps, on a level's settings, the plant's Internode Length and Gravitropism, and a flower component's inflorescence settings, are read per branch, node or flower while the plant grows. Their effects pass through the physics.
  • Instance maps, on a component's Size, Pitch, Yaw, Roll, Fold and petiole settings, are read per drawn leaf or flower after the plant is grown.
  • Per-plant maps cover every other setting, which is one value for the whole plant. They draw one random value per plant through the curve. In a row of Variations each plant gets its own value.

A Random Range on a setting is a per-part random spread around it. On a setting that used to have a +/- variance, the Random Range is that variance, so older plants are unchanged.

Why maps and not more sliders

Each extra slider is one more number that has to agree with all the others. A map instead says how an existing setting varies over the plant, in terms of something the plant already measures. The setting keeps one meaning, and one map icon beside it shows whether anything varies it.

Bend and droop under load

Explanation

A PlantGen stem bends because it carries weight, not because a slider tells it to. Once the plant has grown, a fixed pass treats every stem and branch as a beam fixed at its base and bends it under the weight it holds. That pass never adds or removes a part. It only changes which way each part points.

What a stem carries

At each node the load is everything beyond it: the stem's own wood above, and every leaf, flower and fruit that stem and its branches carry. A load far out to the side turns the node harder than the same load close in.

The organs' weights come from their components:

  • A leaf weighs its component's Weight times its size squared, since a leaf is a plate.
  • A flower weighs its component's Weight times its size cubed, since a head is a lump. A head twice as big is eight times as heavy.
  • A fruit weighs the fruit component's Weight times its size cubed. A fruiting branch bows more than the same branch in flower.

Weight scales with the organ's own growth, so a bud that has not opened yet hardly loads its stem.

What resists it

A stem's resistance is its Stiffness times its cross-section's resistance to bending, which grows with the fourth power of its radius. A stem twice as thick resists 16 times the bend. That is why a stem stays upright at its thick base and nods at its thin tip under the same head, and why the stem's taper under Width shapes the bend as much as Stiffness does.

Stiffness is set per level and runs on a log scale: each 0.1 doubles it, so 0 to 1 spans a thousand-fold range. Physiology › Stiffness › Preset fills every level from a stem type, from Herbaceous to Woody. A bend can't go tighter than about 15 times the stem's radius, the point where a real tube kinks, so even a very soft stem curves rather than folds.

The two numbers trade off

Weight and Stiffness only mean something together. Measured on a new plant at Day 270 with a single flower at the stem's tip, the tip's angle from vertical:

StiffnessWeight 0.05Weight 0.1Weight 0.2
0.51°3°5°
0.212°22°42°
0.123°44°85°

In this range the angle about doubles when Stiffness drops by 0.1, and about doubles when Weight doubles. Every flower a stem's branches carry loads the stem too: with a flower at all 12 tips of the same plant, Weight 0.01 at Stiffness 0.1 already turns the stem's tip 119°. On a small, light plant there is little mass, so the bend stays small until Stiffness is low.

Flower stalks

A flower's own stalk, the pedicel, sags by the same beam rule: the flower's weight at its end, against the stalk's length and thickness. A long thin stalk under a heavy flower hangs; a short thick one holds the flower out.

The pedicel's Angle and Bend are not weights. They set the angle the stalk leaves at and the curve it grows with, whatever the flower weighs, and the sag adds to them. Use them when flowers should point a certain way on any plant, like the bells of a hanging raceme. A flower component's Orientation (Erect, Horizontal, Pendulous and others), with its Strength, aims the inflorescence's flowers the same way.

Gravitropism is growth, not bend

Gravitropism in Physiology › Tropisms acts while the plant grows: each new node steers back toward upright. It changes where the stem goes, and the bend then acts on that. Autotropism straightens older stem tissue after growth, so a mature stem is tidy while its youngest nodes keep their nod.

When a bend seems dead

It is almost always one of three things. The stem is too stiff for the load. The organ is too light, because its component's Weight is low or its Size is small and Weight goes with the square or cube of Size. Or the load sits near the stem's thick base, where the fourth-power radius term wins. The bend debug views in Debug Tools show the load, stiffness and moment at every node.

The environment nudges, it doesn't decide

Explanation

A PlantGen plant can respond to light, obstacles and effectors. None of them decide its shape. The species' own growth decides how many stems, branches, leaves and flowers there are and where they sit. The surroundings only change a number that growth was already using, such as which way a tip is heading. Nothing in the environment creates a part, places one, or ends an axis outright.

Why it works this way

An early PlantGen grew branches toward open space, the way tree generators fill a crown. The surroundings then decided where branches went, when they forked and when they stopped, and the species settings shrank to decoration. Every plant came out as the same shape at a different size. A perennial's form is mostly its own program: a foxglove is a spike whether it stands in a field or by a wall. So the environment was made to bend that program, not to write it.

What each one changes

All of these are in Physiology:

  • Light Seeking (Light) turns growing tips toward the light each step, after gravity has had its say. The light comes from a coarse grid of the plant's surroundings, where the plant's own leaves and stems and the obstacles cast shade.
  • Heliotropism with its own Sun Object (each flower component's Inflorescence box) turns that component's flowers toward the object after growth, each flower's own stalk curving with it as one even arc, no joint turning more than 7 degrees. Leaf Heliotropism turns leaf blades toward the plant's Sun Object (Light).
  • Clearance (Obstacles) curves tips away from the meshes in the obstacle Collection as they come within that distance. A tip that runs out of room stops rather than grows through; that is the one case where the surroundings end an axis, and only because the space is solid.
  • Effectors pull, push, flatten or twist growth near an empty you place (Grow around obstacles and steer with effectors).
  • Shade Death (Senescence) judges the finished plant: a branch whose base ends up darker than the threshold dies, with everything it carries. Stems are never killed this way. It runs after growth, on the finished plant's own shade, so it doesn't change how the rest of the plant grew.

Off means exactly off

Every one of these starts at 0, or empty. At 0 the plant is byte-for-byte the same as one grown with no surroundings at all, and the light grid is not even built. PlantGen builds it only when something reads it: Light Seeking, Shade Death, or a mask or map on the Shade channel.

Obstacles and effectors are read in the plant's own space, so moving the plant next to a rock is the same as moving the rock. Neither move regrows the plant on its own. Click Regrow after moving one.

Inflorescence types

Explanation

A flower component's Type picks how its flowers are arranged: a single flower, a raceme, an umbel, a cyme and so on. The list is long, but the types fall into a few families that grow in genuinely different ways. Knowing the family tells you which settings will matter.

Three separate questions

Three settings in three places decide where a plant flowers and how, and they are easy to confuse:

  • Attachment Location, on the flower component, says where an inflorescence starts: at the tips (Terminal), at the nodes (Axillary, Internodal, Leaf-opposed), from old wood (Cauliflorous, Ramiflorous), or from the ground (Basal).
  • Type, on the same component, says what grows there: one flower, or a stalk of many in a given arrangement.
  • Growth Pattern, on a level, says how the plant's leafy axes carry on. It shapes the stems, not the inflorescence. A sympodial stem and a cyme both relay, but one is the plant's frame and the other is its flowering head.

The families

One flower. Solitary puts a single flower at each place the component takes. The flower's look is all in its mesh.

Flowers along a continuing axis. Raceme, Spike, Corymb and Verticillaster grow a flowering stalk that keeps extending, with flowers along it, oldest at the bottom. They differ in the details: a raceme's flowers have stalks (pedicels), a spike's sit on the axis, a corymb's lower stalks are longer so the flowers reach one level, and a verticillaster puts its flowers in rings with a pair of bracts under each and bare stem between. The settings that matter are flower Spacing, Count, the Pedicel fold and Bloom order.

Flowers from one point. Umbel and Flat Umbel radiate every pedicel from the tip. A flat umbel's pedicels are worked out so every flower lands on one plane, as in a cow parsley head. Pedicel length and Spread shape it.

Branched heads. Panicle is a branched raceme: the axis carries branches, and the branches carry the flowers. The compound types, Compound Spike, Compound Corymb, Compound Umbel and Compound Flat Umbel, repeat their own arrangement one level down, so each flower position holds a small copy of the whole head. The Branching fold (Depth and the branch settings) matters here.

Relayed chains. The cymes end differently from everything above. Their tip flowers first and stops, and new shoots from below it carry on and flower in turn. Scorpioid and Helicoid cymes relay with one shoot, zig-zagging or spiralling; a Dichasium relays with two, forking at every spent flower; a Pleiochasium with a ring of three or more. Cyme (custom) exposes the relay settings directly. A cyme opens in the order it grows: with Bloom order on Middle first (what picking a cyme sets), the tip flower opens first and each relay generation one step later, so a dichasium of depth 3 runs 0, 1/3, 2/3, 1 along the bloom timeline. Outside first reverses it.

Catkins. Catkin is the one type a stem does not turn into. The twigs go on being twigs and hang catkins on short stalks along their length, as hazel and willow do.

None grows no flowers, for a foliage plant.

Picking a type sets other settings

Choosing a Type fills several flower settings with values that suit it, such as the pedicel length, spacing and branching for a compound head. Tune them after choosing. Changing the Type replaces them, so pick the type first.

The generated Inflorescence types table in the reference lists every type with its description.

Seeds and the same plant twice

Explanation

A PlantGen plant is random in its details and exact as a whole. The same settings and the same seed grow the same plant, bit for bit, every time. A different seed grows a sibling: the same species, a different individual.

What a seed changes

Every random choice in the plant, such as a branch's exact angle, how long one stem grows, or which mesh a leaf takes, is drawn from the seeds. The settings set the ranges; the seed picks inside them.

On the Generic perennial at Day 270, five master seeds give five plants with the same 12 axes and 89 nodes, standing between 0.47 m and 0.61 m tall. The structure is the species. The lean, the lengths and the exact angles are the individual.

Master Seed and the part seeds

The Master Seed in Plant Generator reshuffles everything. Every level and every component also has its own Seed, mixed with the master:

  • A level's Seed reshuffles that level's draws: its branches' angles, lengths and which nodes fork.
  • A component's Seed reshuffles which mesh each point takes and its jitter in size and rotation.

At 0, a level or component follows the master alone, and that is the default. Changing one part's seed leaves the others' draws alone. Setting the Generic plant's branch level to Seed 7 changes every branch, and its stem grows exactly as before. The stem still moves, by 0.4 mm at most, because the reshuffled branches load it slightly differently.

Why draws are tied to parts, not order

Each draw is keyed on the part it belongs to, never on the order the code happens to reach it. Two consequences follow.

First, adding a component doesn't reshuffle what's already there. A leaf placed on a stem keeps its look because its draw comes from where it sits on the plant, not from its number in a list. That's what lets a timelapse grow a leaf in without the leaves around it flickering.

Second, settings that change when parts are made would deal every later part a different hand. So timing controls like Emergence Delay don't change when parts are made; they change when they're shown. The full-grown plant stays the same whatever the delay.

Practical use

  • To pick between individuals, use Variations: a row of the same plant on seeds 100, 200, 300 and so on, side by side.
  • To keep a plant you like while trying other settings, leave its seeds alone. Seeds are saved with the plant and in its preset.
  • To vary only one part, change that level's or component's Seed instead of the Master Seed.

The rig and Unreal's wind

Explanation

PlantGen exports a plant to a game engine as a skeletal mesh, and lets the engine do the swaying. This page explains why the rig is built the way it is and what the wind file actually tells Unreal.

Why the engine animates, not PlantGen

A baked wind animation loops the same few seconds, ignores the scene's wind direction, and costs memory per plant. Unreal's Dynamic Wind instead simulates the sway live from the skeleton, for one global wind. What it needs from us is not motion but a description: which bones form chains, and how freely each group moves. So Export Rig writes the mesh in its rest pose and a wind file that classifies the bones. Nothing moving is exported.

How the bones are placed

A bone per node would be thousands of bones on a leafy perennial. A bone per stem would sway as a stiff stick. The rig sits between the two by asking two questions of each stretch of stem:

  • Shape. A bone runs on while every node it covers stays within the level's Bone Angle of the bone's line. A straight run shares one bone; a curve gets more.
  • Flex. It also stops where the stem would turn more than the Bone Angle under its own weight pushed sideways, the same beam rule the bend pass uses. A thin, flexible tip gets more bones than a thick base of the same shape, because that's where the sway is.

A bone chain also breaks wherever a branch leaves, so each branch hangs off a bone that ends at its base. Every drawn leaf, bract, flower, bud and fruit gets one bone from its stalk's root to its far end, under the stem bone carrying it.

The exception is flowers that share an axis. They have no bone of their own and ride the stem bone at their node, so a raceme sways as one piece. A flowering tree needs this: Laburnum's 29,595 flowers were 62% of a 47,400-bone rig. A lone flower head, such as Rudbeckia's, keeps its bone and nods on its own stalk.

How the mesh follows the bones

Each vertex follows at most four bones. Along a stem, two neighbouring bones blend across each joint so it bends smoothly. A branch is handed over from its parent's bones to its own over a short distance from the parent's surface, so the junction doesn't tear. A stalk's foot is handed over to its organ's bone the same way. Which bone a vertex belongs to is worked out from the geometry and the grown plant, not from the welded mesh's labels, which are unreliable at junctions.

What the wind file says

The wind file puts every bone in one simulation group:

  • Trunk: the root and every stem bone within 16 bones of it, at any level, plus any run of fewer than 8 bones deeper than that.
  • Branches: the other stem bones deeper than that, at influence 0.
  • Organs 1 to 4: every leaf, flower and fruit bone, sorted by how free the stem bone it hangs from is.

The trunk is where the depth rule matters. Dynamic Wind bends trunk bones along one smooth, slow line, and that bend adds up from bone to bone, so the limit is a line's depth and never its level. Other groups give each bone its own noise and a fast oscillation. Stems jittered there at every influence tried: a two-bone side stem at any value, and Laburnum and Corylus branches down to a maximum of 0.01. So the deep stems get no wind of their own and ride their parent, which moves a tree's outer wood as a whole. A perennial's stems are all on the trunk. On Corylus, 1,779 bones are and 2,213 outer branch bones ride.

An organ's influence is the flexibility of the bone it hangs from, relative to the most flexible stem bone in the plant, scaled by 0.35. The file's gust attenuation starts from one minus the mean flexibility of the level 0 stems, so a stiff plant shrugs off gusts that move a lax one. Past 10 bones on the longest trunk line, the gust that gets through is shared over the line's bones, because more bones would otherwise mean more sway: Araucaria's 17 bones went from 0.6 to 0.765.

Because the groups come from the same beam model as the bend, a plant that droops easily in PlantGen sways easily in Unreal.

The previews

Bone Wind in Blender approximates what Unreal will do: each stem bone bends by its own flexibility times a gust. Since the bend comes from the stem's own flexibility, the sway depends on how long and stiff the stems are, not on how many bones they have. Its Strength, Stiffness and Gust settings exist only for the preview; Unreal has its own.

Vertex Wind previews the leaf flutter a foliage material makes from the vertex colours. Engines do that in the material, so it is not exported either.

Fast Preview keeps playback quick. A deforming mesh costs Blender most in redrawing it, about 130 ms a frame for a 250,000-vertex plant. So Rig View deforms only the stems and moves the leaves and flowers as rigid copies with their bones. On the plants it was measured on, the shape matches the full mesh to 0.001 mm and playback runs 2 to 2.7 times faster. It falls back to the full mesh while Vertex Wind is on, and the export always uses the full mesh.

Fuse Petals To Tubecheckbox
default off

Widen each petal's base until they tile the tube's mouth exactly, closing the gaps between them so the corolla reads as one piece rather than separate lobes stuck to a cylinder. Fades back into the petal's own outline just above the mouth, so it doesn't override the Petal Shape

Flip Normalscheckbox
default off

Turn the corolla tube's faces the other way round (the front becomes the back)

Plant Effector

panel

Shown when an effector empty is selected. Its settings steer the growth of every plant whose Effectors collection holds it.

Kindchoice
default Attract

How this effector biases growth

Attract

Pull nearby growth toward this point, fading out at the radius

Repel

Push nearby growth away from this point, fading out at the radius

Forbid

Keep growth out of this sphere entirely. Tips lean away as they approach and any that still reach the boundary stop there, the same way they stop at a wall

Target

Aim growth at this point from anywhere, with no falloff. A training goal for a whole plant rather than a local magnet - Radius is ignored

Flatten

Grow in the plane this effector faces, for an espalier or a fan. Rotate the effector to turn the plane. Radius is how far either side of the plane the flattening reaches

Orbit

Spiral growth around this effector's axis, for a stem twining up a pole. Rotate the effector to aim the axis. Radius is how far out from the axis it reaches. Pair it with an Attract on the same spot to keep the stem against the pole

Align Up

Turn each node's frame to face this effector, so the leaves and flowers on it swing round - put one where the sun is and the foliage follows. It turns where branches leave the stem too, so on a bushy plant the whole shape shifts, not just the foliage. Reads strongest on opposite, distichous or unilateral species: a spiral keeps its leaves spread all round the stem and simply rotates the whole set

Level Up

Turn each node's frame to lie flat in this effector's plane. Same reach as Align Up - foliage and branch angles both. Rotate the effector to turn the plane

Radiusnumber
default 0.3 m · 0 m to ∞

Sphere of influence. The pull fades to nothing at this distance. Ignored by Target, which reaches everywhere

Strengthnumber
default 0.3 · 0 to 1

How far a growing tip turns toward or away from this effector each step. 1 aims it straight at the effector every step, which is as strong as this can get - there is nothing above it

Components

panel

The plant's structure in one tree: its branching levels, and the leaf, bract, flower, bud and fruit components placed on them. The selected row's settings show below the tree.

Listlist

The Plant Structure tree: the Plant, the levels and the components placed on them, each row with its guide lines. Double-click (or F2) a name to rename it; the box on the right shows or mutes it.

Level settingsfold

Phyllotaxischoice
default Alternate (spiral) · shown for branch levels

How this level's branches are arranged round their parent -- sets Spiral, Whorl and Whorl Angle. On the stems level the stems fill the base as a phyllotactic disc, each turned the golden angle (or Whorl Angle) from the last

Custom

Spiral and whorl set by hand

Alternate (spiral)

One per node on a golden spiral (137.5 deg)

Distichous

One per node, alternating 180 deg -- two ranks

Opposite

A pair at each node, stacked up the stem

Decussate

A pair at each node, each turned 90 deg from the last

Whorled

Three per node, each whorl turned half a step

Spiral Anglenumbermappable
default 137.5 · 0 to 360 · shown for branch levels

Degrees each node turns round the parent from the last

Arrangement
Stemswhole numbermappable
default 1 · 1 to 8 on the slider (1 to ∞ typed)

Branches per node, spaced round the parent. On the stems level: how many stems

Growth
Growth Patternchoice
default Monopodial

How this level's axes carry their growth on: one apex, relays from units that end, or a tip that splits

Monopodial

One apex builds the whole axis; its branches come off its sides

Sympodial

The axis grows in units: each ends (Unit End) and one bud below it carries on -- a zig-zag chain

Dichasial

Each unit ends and two buds carry on: a false fork with the spent tip in every crotch

Pleiochasial

Each unit ends and a ring of Relays buds carries on

Pseudomonopodial (Aligned Relay)

A sympodium whose relay continues in line, the spent tip pushed aside: one straight stem with side-set flowers

Dichotomous

The growing tip splits into equal forks

Pseudomonopodial (Unequal Fork)

The tip splits unequally: a leader carries on, weaker forks peel off -- a fake trunk

Stepswhole numbermappable
default 12 · 1 to 60 on the slider (1 to ∞ typed)

Nodes the axis has when fully grown. A flowering axis flowers after them

Growthnumbermappable
default 100% · 1% to 100%

How much of its Steps each axis of this level builds. A branch at 50% is the lower half of the full one, not a smaller copy (its taper and maps stay put), the last node grown partly, and it still flowers at its cut tip. Map it to vary it per branch

Emergence Delaywhole numbermappable
default 0 · 0 to 30 on the slider (0 to ∞ typed)

Growth steps each branch of this level waits after the node it leaves forms before it starts growing (on a stems level: steps after the plant starts). Timing only: the full-grown plant is unchanged -- the plant's season lengthens to fit -- so it shows at earlier Days and in Grow Over Timeline. Map it to stagger branches

Seedwhole number
default 0 · 0 to 2147483647 on the slider (0 to ∞ typed)

This level's own seed, on top of the plant's: changing it redraws only this level's variation (length, width, slide, fork chance, mask survival). 0 follows the plant's seed alone

Length
Start (m)numbermappable
default 1 · 0 to 2 on the slider (0 to ∞ typed)

First internode, as a fraction of the parent's internode where the branch attaches

Per Stepnumbermappable
default 1 · 0 to 1.5 on the slider (0 to ∞ typed)

Each internode is this times the one before -- below 1 shortens toward the tip

Width
Radius (m)numbermappable
default 1 · 0 to 2 on the slider (0 to ∞ typed)

Base width, as a fraction of the parent's width where the branch attaches

Per Stepnumbermappable
default 1 · 0 to 1.5 on the slider (0 to ∞ typed)

Each node's width is this times the one before -- below 1 tapers

Stiffnessnumbermappable
default 0.75 · 0 to 1

How strongly this level's stems or branches resist bending under their load: a real material stiffness (Young's modulus) on a log scale, 0 is 5 MPa, 0.5 is 160 MPa, 1 is 5 GPa. Soft herbaceous stems sit around 0.1-0.4, grass culms and woody stems around 0.8-1. Thick parts already resist far more than thin ones, so raising this mostly straightens the tips

Cross Sectionchoice
default Circular

The shape swept along this level's stems or branches. A botanical trait as much as an artistic one - a square stem says mint family, a triangular one says sedge

Circular

A round stem, the usual case

Triangular

Three-sided - sedges have edges

Square

Four-sided, diagnostic of the mint family

Hexagonal

Six-sided

Polygonal

A regular polygon with a side count you set

Flattened

Squashed across one axis, like a ribbon or a flattened grass culm

Winged

A few deep ridges running the length of the stem

Ribbed

Many shallow ridges, like celery or angelica

Star

Deep sharp points

Spiral

Degrees the growing tip bends each step
